strengths: Clear and well-motivated insight that output length should be modeled as a distribution rather than point estimates, matching the stochastic nature of LLM decoding
Solid theoretical analysis with Theorem 3.2 establishing power-law decay of output length under reasonable assumptions
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple models (8 variants), datasets (3 real/synthetic), and scenarios (online/offline) showing consistent improvements of 2.31× over SSJF
Convincing distribution fitting analysis with 93.1% KS pass rate for log-t distribution, compared against alternative heavy-tailed distributions
Practical implementation with asynchronous prediction and dynamic batching demonstrating systems-level considerations; minimal scheduling overhead (4.26ms per request)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: log-t distribution fitting is standard statistical modeling; CVaR for risk-sensitive scheduling is a well-known finance technique; the scheduling rule Score=E[X]+β·CVaR is trivial. The combination lacks conceptual depth for a top venue.

Significant experimental fairness issues: (1) TIE uses 45K samples with 20 repetitions vs 900K unique samples for baselines, making 'equal training data scale' claim misleading since distribution fitting may be easier than regression; (2) Different predictor models (BERT-base vs OPT-125M vs DeBERTa-v3-base) make unclear whether improvements come from scheduling or stronger encoder; (3) Different training procedures (two-stage vs standard) for different methods

Assumption 3.1 is underutilized and unvalidated: the assumption f(p)~c·p^(α-1) is never empirically verified; Theorem 3.2 is only for theoretical justification and the method doesn't depend on it; 6.9% of prompts fail KS test with no analysis of these failure cases

Critical missing baselines: No comparison with TRAIL or ELIS (iterative methods mentioned in introduction) that make different latency-accuracy trade-offs; only comparing with non-adaptive methods (SSJF, LTR) is insufficient

Absence of statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance testing, or multiple runs reported; impossible to assess statistical significance of improvements; variance across experimental repetitions not provided

Table 4 ablation reveals questionable value of distribution modeling: using only E[X] (SEPT) achieves 0.75s vs 0.67s for full TIE (10% improvement); most gains come from adaptive β weighting, not the distribution modeling itself, contradicting paper's core claim

Ad-hoc hyperparameter design: β adaptation formula (Eq. 12) uses apparently arbitrary constants [0.1, 0.5] without justification; α=0.9 for CVaR fixed without sensitivity analysis; γ=0.9, τ=30s for starvation prevention are defaults with no ablation

Training data collection practical limitation acknowledged in Appendix E but not adequately addressed: requiring multiple generations per prompt for fitting creates a production deployment bottleneck that generalization claims don't eliminate

Incomplete analysis and missing insights: No failure case breakdown, no prediction error analysis, no correlation between prediction accuracy and scheduling improvements, no investigation of why distribution modeling helps beyond enabling β weighting

strengths: Well-motivated insight that output lengths are inherently uncertain and should be modeled as distributions rather than point estimates, directly addressing a real limitation of existing methods
Rigorous distribution analysis with Theorem 3.2 providing theoretical justification for heavy-tailed output lengths, and strong empirical validation of log-t distribution (93.1% KS pass rate)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 3 datasets, 9 models, both online/offline scenarios, with extensive ablations and cross-dataset/model generalization tests demonstrating consistent improvements (2.31× latency, 1.42× throughput)
Thoughtful practical implementation including asynchronous prediction with dynamic batching, showing understanding of deployment constraints in continuous batching systems
Strong and consistent empirical results that hold across diverse settings, with clear breakdowns of where performance gains originate
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines well-established techniques (log-t distributions from Cassidy et al. 2010, CVaR from Rockafellar et al. 2000, SJF scheduling). Theorem 3.2 is a straightforward application of dominated convergence theorem without substantial new theoretical insight.

Significant practical limitation is under-emphasized: requires multiple generations per prompt (20×45K=900K generations) for data collection. Point-estimate baselines (SSJF/LTR) can use production logs directly. This data collection overhead is substantial and may limit adoption, especially for smaller operators or newly deployed models.

Core Assumption 3.1 (termination rate distribution f(p)∼c·p^(α-1)) lacks rigorous empirical validation. While Appendix D.4 shows heavy tails, it does not directly verify the assumed functional form. Theorem 3.2 critically depends on this unvalidated assumption.

Design choices lack principled justification: α=0.9 for CVaR (why top 10%?), β adaptive formula with specific ranges (Eq. 12), ν=3.5 fixed, γ=0.9 and τ=30s all appear somewhat arbitrary with minimal sensitivity analysis or ablation beyond Table 4.

Incomplete baseline comparison: only TRAIL examined from preemptive scheduling methods (Appendix D.8, briefly). Paper acknowledges preemptive scheduling as alternative but doesn't thoroughly explore it. ELIS is mentioned but not compared.

Mixed generalization across model families (Table 5): DeepSeek-R1 shows only 1.3-1.8× improvement vs 3-4× for other models; Qwen3-Next-80B shows inconsistency between metrics. Raises questions about universality of approach.
Weak prediction model: only DeBERTa-base + MLP (R²=0.76 for σ). No comparison with stronger encoders or alternative architectures. No ablation on feature extraction (CLS + mean + max pooling).
Statistical rigor absent: no confidence intervals or significance tests. Are 2.31× improvements statistically significant? Results lack error bars across multiple experimental runs.

Prediction vs baseline fairness question: SSJF/LTR trained on 900K single samples; TIE trained on 45K×20 multiple samples. While total generation count matches, sampling strategy differs. Missing ablation: would distributions improve SSJF/LTR as well?

Overhead analysis superficial: 4.26ms per request claimed negligible, but scalability unclear at higher RPS. Monte Carlo sampling with 10k samples—sensitivity to this choice unexplored. Streaming responses and variable max_tokens not addressed.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated insight: Modeling output length as a distribution rather than point estimate elegantly captures the stochastic nature of LLM decoding, with compelling motivation in Figure 1

Strong theoretical contribution: Theorem 3.2 rigorously justifies heavy-tailed output length distributions under reasonable Assumption 3.1; interpretations (JSON/code generation, detailed explanations) are intuitive

Comprehensive empirical validation: Log-t distribution achieves 93.1% KS pass rate; extensive testing across 9 models from different families, 3 datasets, online/offline workloads, with good cross-model and cross-dataset generalization (Table 2)

Thorough ablation studies: Distribution family, score components, sample size, ν parameter, prompt types, training data scale, temperature, adaptive β, and robustness systematically evaluated (Tables 4, 7-12)
Substantial practical improvements: 2.31× per-token latency speedup (online) and 1.42× throughput gains (offline); graceful degradation under load (3.68× vs 6-8.5× for baselines)
Practical implementation: Asynchronous prediction with dynamic batching avoids blocking; negligible overhead (4.26ms scheduling vs 48.23s TTFT)
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective architectural diagrams (Figures 2-3) and heatmaps (Figure 5) clearly demonstrating improved request clustering
Honest limitations discussion: Training data requirements and future directions transparently acknowledged in Section 7
weaknesses: Assumption 3.1 validation gap: Termination rate density f(p) ∼ c·p^(α-1) is not directly validated—paper shows empirically that outputs are heavy-tailed (supporting conclusion) but doesn't demonstrate the assumed termination rate distribution, creating some circularity in the argument

Training data requirement: Unlike SSJF/LTR learning from production logs, TIE requires offline collection of 45K prompts × 20 generations. While Appendix D.5 shows competitive performance at lower data scales, this collection cost limits real-time adaptation and deployment ease

Prediction quality asymmetry: R² = 0.76 for σ prediction notably lower than μ (0.82). Table 12 shows graceful robustness, but lower σ quality may limit effectiveness; more analysis of σ prediction error sources needed

Heuristic design choices lack principled justification: Adaptive β formula (Eq. 12) and starvation decay mechanism (Score' = Score·γ^(t_w/τ)) work empirically but appear ad-hoc. Why [0.1,0.5]? Why γ=0.9, τ=30s? Could benefit from theoretical derivation
Limited preemptive scheduling comparison: TRAIL baseline (Table 11) only in appendix. While TIE scales better, TRAIL outperforms at low load (≤40 RPS); this tradeoff deserves main text discussion

Incomplete distribution sensitivity: Only log-t, log-normal, Gamma, Weibull, Exponential tested. Pareto or other heavy-tailed families not compared. Sensitivity to CVaR confidence level α (fixed at 0.9) not explored
Missing comparisons: No comparison with optimal scheduling (known output lengths), quantile regression baselines, or other heavy-tailed distribution families; would strengthen evaluation
Generalization across decoding parameters: Temperature sensitivity explored (Table 9), but top-p, beam width, other decoding variations not tested; robustness to different decoding strategies unclear
